shownK(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    ZZ32 => v.asString || " : ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => v.asString || " : ZZ64"
    NN32 => v.asString || " : NN32"
    RR64 => v.asString || " : RR64"
    else => v.asString || " : other"
  end

object BoxK[\T\](v: T)
  accept(x: T): String = shownK(x)
end

scaleK[\T\](b: BoxK[\T\], x: T): String = b.accept(x)
sameK[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): String = "[" shownK(a) ", " shownK(b) "]"
sameAddK[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): String = shownK(a + b) " from [" shownK(a) ", " shownK(b) "]"
lohiK[\I extends AnyIntegral\](lo: I, hi: I): String = "[" shownK(lo) ", " shownK(hi) "]"
twiceK[\T extends Integral[\T\]\](a: T, b: T): String = shownK(a + b) " from [" shownK(a) ", " shownK(b) "]"
pickK[\T\](a: T, b: T): String = "[" shownK(a) ", " shownK(b) "]"
ogK[\T\](b: BoxK[\T\], x: T): String = "ogK generic " b.accept(x)
ogK(b: String, x: String): String = "ogK strings"
opK[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): String = "opK generic [" shownK(a) ", " shownK(b) "]"
opK(a: Any, b: Any): String = "opK plain [" shownK(a) ", " shownK(b) "]"

run() = do
    z: ZZ32 = 3
    w: ZZ64 = widen(4)
    l: ZZ64 = widen(7)
    r: RR64 = 2.5
    u: NN32 = unsigned(5)
    b: BoxK[\RR64\] = BoxK[\RR64\](1.0)
    assert(scaleK(b, r), "2.5 : RR64", "control: an RR64 for T fixed at RR64 by BoxK[\\RR64\\]")
    assert(scaleK(b, z), "3.0 : RR64", "row 388: T fixed at RR64 by b, z converted at binding; conversions-coercions.tex:119-120, :430-432")
    assert(scaleK(b, 3), "3.0 : RR64", "row 388: T fixed at RR64 by b, the numeral converted at binding; conversions-coercions.tex:119-120, :430-432")
    assert(sameK(z, z), "[3 : ZZ32, 3 : ZZ32]", "control: two ZZ32 arguments keep T = ZZ32")

\section{Intersection and Union Types}
\seclabel{internal-types}

For every finite set of types, there is a type denoting a unique
\emph{intersection} of those types.
The intersection of a set of types $S$ is a subtype of every type $T \in S$
and of the intersection of every subset of $S$.
There is also a type denoting a unique \emph{union}
of those types. The union of a set of types $S$ is a supertype of every
type $T \in S$ and of the union of every subset of $S$.
Neither intersection types nor union types are first-class types;
they are used solely for type inference (as described in
  \chapref{type-inference}) and
they cannot be expressed directly in programs.

The intersection of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
any subtype of every type $T \in S$ and of the intersection of every
subset of $S$ is a subtype of $U$.
Similarly, the union of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
any supertype of every type $T \in S$ and of the union of every
subset of $S$ is a supertype of $U$.
For example:
%trait S comprises {U,V} end
%trait T comprises {V,W} end
%trait U extends S excludes W end
%trait V extends {S,T} end
%trait W extends T end

   568	\section{Intersection and Union Types}
   569	\seclabel{internal-types}
       
   570	For every finite set of types, there is a type denoting a unique
   571	\emph{intersection} of those types.
   572	The intersection of a set of types $S$ is a subtype of every type $T \in S$
   573	and of the intersection of every subset of $S$.
   574	There is also a type denoting a unique \emph{union}
   575	of those types. The union of a set of types $S$ is a supertype of every
   576	type $T \in S$ and of the union of every subset of $S$.
   577	Neither intersection types nor union types are first-class types;
   578	they are used solely for type inference (as described in
   579	  \chapref{type-inference}) and
   580	they cannot be expressed directly in programs.
       
--- literals 73-96
       
    73	\note{We may want to eliminate the distinction between simple and compound numerals,
    74	and just distinguish them by whether they have a radix point or not, when necessary
    75	(i.e., ``Numerals may have a radix point.'').  Again,
    76	that distinction is primarily a syntactic one, and can be discussed there if appropriate.}
    77	Numeric literals in Fortress are referred to as \emph{numerals},
    78	corresponding to various expressible numbers.
    79	Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
    80	(as described in \secref{numerals}).
       
    81	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
    82	has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
    83	interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
    84	the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
    85	\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
    86	have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?
       
    87	What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
    88	and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?
       
    89	We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
    90	All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
    91	And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
    92	}
--- literals 136-150
   136	converting it immediately to a floating-point number
   137	may lose precision.
   138	If that numeral is used in an expression
   139	involving floating-point intervals,
   140	it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
   141	Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
   142	This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
   143	interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
   144	(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
   145	in Fortress).
   146	\Library\ define coercions
   147	from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
   148	and rational numbers (for compound numerals).

--- cc 488-560
   488	from excludes $U$:
   489	\[
   490	T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
   491	\]
   492	Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.
   493	
   494	We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
   495	\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
   496	coerced to, and rejects $U$:
   497	\[
   498	T \morespecificeq U \iff
   499	T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
   500	(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
   501	\]
   502	
   503	The $\morespecificeq$ relation is reflexive and antisymmetric but not
   504	necessarily transitive.  It is possible, for example, for
   505	three types, $T$, $U$ and $V$, each excluding the other two,
   506	to have coercions from $T$ to $U$ and from $U$ to $V$.  In
   507	this case, $T \morespecificeq U$ and $U \morespecificeq V$ but
   508	$T \not\morespecificeq V$.
   509	
   510	Notice that if two tuple types have a bijective correspondence
   511	between their element types then the $\morespecificeq$ relationship between
   512	the tuple types is equivalent to applying the $\morespecificeq$
   513	relation elementwise.
   514	
   515	We say that $T$ is \emph{more specific} than $U$, and write $T
   516	\morespecific U$, if $T \morespecificeq U \logicand T \neq U$.
   517	
   518	We extend the definitions of no less specific and more specific to
   519	declarations.  We say that a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
   520	specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecificeq \Qs$.
   521	Similarly, we say that a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
   522	specific} than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps)
   523	\morespecificeq (\Qs_0, \Qs)$.  A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more
   524	specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$.
   525	Similarly, a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than
   526	a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps) \morespecific (\Qs_0,
   527	\Qs)$.
   528	
   529	Now we describe how to determine which coercion is applied to a given
   530	call in terms of rewriting functional calls.  The rewriting is
   531	for pedagogical purposes; implementation techniques may vary.
   532	
   533	Consider a static call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$.  Let $\Sigma$ be
   534	the set of parameter types of functional declarations of $\f$ that are
   535	applicable to the call.
   536	Let $\Sigma'$ be the set of parameter types of
   537	functional declarations of $\f$ that are
   538	applicable with coercion to the call.
   539	If $\Sigma$ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution
   540	described in \secref{resolving-overloading} to determine which
   541	element of $\Sigma$ is called.
   542	If $\Sigma$ is empty but $\Sigma'$ is not, then we rewrite the call as
   543	follows.  Define: \[\mathpzc{C} = \{T \in \Sigma' \mid S \coercedefto T
   544	\logicand \As \Ovrsubtype S\}.\] Let $T \in \mathpzc{C}$ be the most
   545	specific element of $\mathpzc{C}$.  In other words, there does not exist
   546	$T' \in \mathpzc{C}$ such that $T' \morespecific T$.  The restrictions
   547	given in \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
   548	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
   549	exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
   550	rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
   551	\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
   552	and the declaration with parameter
   553	type $T$ is applied to the call.
   554	
   555	As an example, consider the following definitions:
   556	%trait ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 } end
   557	%trait ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }
   558	%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
   559	%end
   560	%trait ZZ128

    36	
    37	A \emph{range expression} is used to create a special kind of \TYP{Generator} for
    38	a set of integers, called a \TYP{Range}, useful
    39	for indexing an array or controlling a \KWD{for} loop.  Generators in
    40	general are discussed further in \secref{generators}.
    41	
    42	An \emph{explicit range}
    43	is self-contained and completely describes a set of integers.  Its
    44	components are values of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}: assume that
    45	$a$, $b$, and $c$ are expressions that produce such values.
    46	An integer numeral converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{literals}), and a
    47	\KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter (\secref{natparams}) used as a component
    48	converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does; it is a static error
    49	if any other component of an explicit range has an integer type other than
    50	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
    51	\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's first revision of this section
    52	(\secref{revival-ranges}) left open whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may
    53	appear wherever a variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}),
    54	may be a component of a range.
    55	The sentence above settles it, as both implementations of the revival already
    56	run it: the compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used
    57	as a value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a
    58	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.}
    59	
    60	\begin{itemize}
    61	\item The range \EXP{a\COLONOP{}b} is the set of $n=\max(0,b-a+1)$ integers $\{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b-2, b-1, b\}$.
    62	This is a \emph{nonstrided} range.

All four rungs were approved, and each landed as one commit composed from its branch's net change; no branch is a parent of anything on `main`.

I, then K, then T, then M. No path is shared by two branches (`git diff --name-only bce66f1fa...<branch>` for the four, compared: no path in two lists), so the rule of the lowest edited line in a shared file does not order them, and the batch record's own order stands (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-N.md` section 4, "The order the gather applies them": "no file is shared, so the order matters only for the folds and T's check: I, then K, then T, then M"). content.content:
14:## 1. The list
18:## 2. What the revision states, and what it does not
34:## 3. Per passage: the original, the new text, the reason, route C
38:### 3.1 The chapter (R1)
46:### 3.2 The ranges sentence (R2)
53:### 3.3 Answer 8's callout (R3)
58:### 3.4 Appendix I's sentences (R4, R5, R6)
64:### 3.5 The entry (R7)
68:## 4. Left, with the reason
85:## 5. Decisions taken inside the rung
87:1. **The chapter has two sections and three callouts.** "The Static Arguments of a Call" (`\seclabel{static-arg-inference}`) with four paragraphs headed Choice, Instantiation, The expected type and Dispatch, and "A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie" (`\seclabel{numeral-default}`), which ends with the not-described list. Rejected: one flat chapter (the numeral rule must be citable once, from the coercion chapter's resolution by rung S, so it gets its own label); a section per step (four sections for about a page). One callout per changed passage group, as rung U placed five: the chapter's opening, the interpreter at dispatch, the result-only parameter at the not-described list. Rejected: one long callout at the head, which would put the interpreter's behaviour and the BottomType behaviours far from what they qualify.
88:2. **The first draft note is replaced; the second is kept whole, at the chapter's end.** The first ("This chapter will include...") is false once the chapter describes the rule; the second holds three open questions, the BottomType one among them, which the brief keeps. Rejected: keeping the first note beside the text (a draft note contradicting the chapter under it); moving the second into the revival's callout (it is the team's text; a note prints in the team's draft voice).
89:3. **The resolution is cited, not restated.** The Choice paragraph says "The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes" and adds only what that section does not say: a declaration with static parameters is applicable if some instance within its bounds is, and is compared on its declared parameter types. Rejected: the judgement's full Resolution paragraph (Σ, Σ′, the uniqueness guarantee), which is the coercion chapter's and rung S's cross-reference.
90:4. **The lone parameter's candidates are named: its arguments' own types and the types they can be coerced to.** The judgement's words, "the narrowest type, under ⪯, that every argument constraining it is substitutable for", read over every type including unions, give no narrowest for a ZZ32 and a ZZ64 (their union and ZZ64 are incomparable under ⪯, since nothing coerces into a union and the union coerces into nothing), which would contradict answer 8. Naming the candidates, as the shadow built them and rung I extends them with the types an argument coerces to (the lookup behind answer 8's ZZ32 with NN32), gives answer 8's ZZ64 in every number case and the union only as the fallback. Rejected: the judgement's sentence alone (ambiguous there); "a type a program can write" (it would give `Number` for a ZZ64 and an RR64, where the checker keeps their union: a discrepancy the chapter would create). The brief's words, "the narrowest of its arguments' types and its bound", name the bound as a candidate too; the chapter reaches the bound only as a type the arguments coerce to (a `Narrow` for `T extends Wide` takes `Wide`) or through "the bounds permit". Rejected: the bound as a candidate of its own, which for a ZZ64 and an RR64 under `T extends Number` gives `Number`, where the checker's first attempt, by subtyping, succeeds with their union and the shadow's coercion attempt, which tries the bound, never runs (`explorations/reviews/inference-rule-shadow.md:23-27`); the one shape where the shadow does try the bound, a call whose first attempt fails on another argument's coercion while the lone parameter's arguments have no narrowest type, is reached by no test on record, and statement 5 of section 6 names it for the gather.
91:5. **The union fallback is stated.** Where no candidate is narrowest (a ZZ64 and an RR64: neither converts into the other, answer 8 keeping ZZ64 into RR64 explicit), the parameter takes the union of the arguments' types, its bounds permitting, and nothing is converted. This is today's inference (the solver binds the join of the lower bounds, a union, `Formula.scala:527`), which the shadow keeps ("otherwise the union stays", `explorations/reviews/inference-rule-shadow.md:27`) and rung I's section does not change; it gives the union types' sentence (L11) its referent. Rejected: leaving the case undescribed, which leaves that sentence pointing at nothing and the case open. The gather checks it against I (section 6, statement 5); walk takes a named common supertype there, which the interpreter's callout does not detail (it says only that walk may run a narrower instance where static types are wider).
92:6. **The expected type's contexts are listed as measured on the checker, and the others named as not described.** The list is measurement D's "Context that is passed" (`explorations/reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/measure-D.md:87-91`), read in the source (section 3.1): a typed variable declaration, a declared return type, a block's last expression where no local declaration precedes it, both branches of an `if … else`; used at tight juxtaposition (rung I's `Operators.scala` edit), a method invocation and an operator (today's). The first pass called it the checker's whole list, and it was not: the first skeptic measured two more contexts the checker keeps on the base, a field declaration with a declared type (`probes/skeptic/SkCtx-base.txt:16-17`, `probes/skeptic/SkCtxField.fss`) and an assignment to a variable of declared type (`:18-19`, `probes/skeptic/SkCtxAssign.fss`), which the coercion chapter's "variable and field declarations" also names (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:117-118`). The repair round adds both (`inference.tex:109-112`) and nothing else: a field assignment was not measured, so the sentence says an assignment to a variable. The seven contexts the checker accepted and the two it refused behave as the chapter now says (`probes/skeptic/SkCtx-base.txt:2-24`). Rejected: the general "wherever the context expects a type" of the coercion chapter's list (`conversions-coercions.tex:115-127`), which would state more than rung I builds (an argument, a `let` body and the rest keep dropping it, measure D section 1.3), the batch's stop. The phrase "where no local declaration precedes it" reads oddly as a language rule; it is what the checker does (`Decls.scala:52-57`, and `SkCtxBlockDecl`, `SkCtx-base.txt:8-11`), and the not-described list names the other case, so the text is exact and open about it.
93:7. **Dispatch is the judgement's sentence, and walk's run-time inference is a callout.** The brief lists "that run-time dispatch infers a dispatched declaration's static arguments by the same rule from the arguments' run-time types (walk's implementation is rung K's; ...)"; the judgement's section 5 gives rung T "a callout that walk applies the same rule from run-time types", and its Dispatch text says "by subtyping and without further coercion". Stated as normative text for both paths, "by the same rule" would contradict "without further coercion" for the compiled path's re-dispatch, where the arguments are already converted and a dispatched generic is instantiated by subtyping, and it would settle row 496's open question ("none settles the run-time answer") beyond what any rung of this batch builds. So the normative Dispatch paragraph is the judgement's sentence, and the interpreter's run-time rule is the second callout. Rejected: the normative sentence (both reasons).
94:8. **The examples are the shapes rung I's tests pin.** `wrap(3)` into `List[\ZZ64\]` and `id(3)` into ZZ64 (I's `a: BoxT[\ZZ64\] = wrapT(3)` and `a: ZZ64 = idt(3)`), ZZ64 for ZZ32 with NN32 (I's), `g(0)` over NN32 and ZZ32 (I's `pickn(3)`), `op(z, w)` (I's and K's `OpAnyZW`). Each is written with names of its own, since the specification names neither `widen` nor `Integral`, and `List`, which it declares, in place of the tests' `BoxT`. Rejected: `O2Z64`'s re-dispatch to `plain64` as the dispatch example: walk refuses its overload set at load until batch 7b's rung W (`OverloadedFunction.java:527`), so it would not run on both paths at the gather.
95:9. **L19, the Effect of "The number types", is left.** Section 4. Rejected: revising it as rung U revised its range half (rung U's decision 8): that sentence had become false; this one has become fulfilled, and the new entry says so.
96:10. **The callout of `basic-integers.tex` keeps its line count**, so no test citation of the chapter moves (rung U's decision 7). Rejected: a rewrap with a pointer to the new section, which would move every citation of the chapter below `:94` in ten test files.
97:11. **"Passages not yet revised" keeps both paragraphs, revised.** The brief says "revised to say the rule is written, keeping the rest of each"; the rule's paragraph now also names the passages the chapter leaves unrevised (L1 to L3), which is that section's purpose, and the `nat` paragraph says the question is settled and where. Rejected: deleting both (the section lists what is unrevised, and after this change the overloading sentences and the implicit bound are); the brief's wording.
98:12. **The ranges sentence names `nat` and `int` parameters "used as a component"** and keeps the static error for "any other component". Pavol's entry names a size (a `nat` parameter); the batch record's section 1 reads it as "a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value", and both paths run an `int` parameter the same way (`probes/examples/SizeAsComponent-base.txt`, S6, S7; `KindEnv.scala:67-68`). Rejected: "used as a value" (the section speaks of components); `nat` alone (the record's reading and the paths' behaviour include `int`).
99:13. **The callouts name the revision of the overloading chapters by its date, not "batch 7b's rung S".** No callout of the specification names a rung or a batch; Appendix I and this record do (this record, section 4; the entry cites this record). Rejected: the rung's name in a box a reader of the specification cannot place.
100:14. **The first callout names the compiled path's own bound, `Object`, with row 412.** The chapter assumes Any, as the library and walk take it; the compile path gives every empty `extends` clause `Object` (row 412), under which a result-only parameter binds BottomType. Rejected: "as the implementations take it", which the compiled path contradicts.
101:15. **The rule is narrowed to type, `nat` and `int` parameters (the repair round, the judge's decision).** The first pass stated the rule for any static parameter a parameter type mentions, which covers `bool`, `dim`, `unit` and operator parameters (L26). Neither implementation infers a `bool` one, the checker refuses `dim` and `unit` by name as well, and no probe measured an operator parameter. The brief gives the chapter the rule "as far as rung I builds it and no further" (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-N.md`, section 3, T, "What it writes"), and normative text stating more than rung I builds is the stop it reserves for Pavol ("Stops"); the judge took the narrowing for that reason (`JUDGE.md` section 3, F1). So the scope sentence (`inference.tex:19-25`) and the first bullet (`:75-79`) name type, `nat` and `int` parameters, the second bullet (`:80-82`) a type parameter only, since the skeptic's context probes and measurement D are over type parameters and no probe shows a size fixed through the expected type, and the not-described list names the static arguments of a `bool`, `dim`, `unit` or operator parameter (`:189-190`) with no behaviour stated. The Working Draft's own `bool` example presumes the inference (L26), so the third callout keeps that presumption in the revival's voice beside both implementations' refusals (`:218-224`), and `XXXNatBoolChecker` keeps its reason. `:15-18`, which says a call need not write its static arguments, is left: it restates the Working Draft's own `Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:35-40` and `method-invocation.tex:49-52`. Rejected: the general rule kept, with the refusals in a callout, which would state the designers' presumption as a rule both paths refuse today and land as a met reserved stop for Pavol's review.
102:16. **Two changes the judge's steps did not list (the repair round).** The entry's Effect said "A declared type fixes a static argument that the return type of a call written as f(x) mentions inside another type" (`changes.tex:1641-1642` before the change); after decision 15 the chapter fixes only a type parameter through the expected type (`inference.tex:80-82`), so the Effect now says "a type parameter", one word, although the judge's step 8 said to change nothing else of the entry: the chapter the entry describes settles it (`JUDGE.md` section 3, F1, gives the same reason for the bullet). And the dispatch example (`inference.tex:141-148`) now names its declarations before its call: the first pass's order left the declaration `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` overrunning the line by 57.97pt, an overfull box the base does not have (the first pass's `probes/build/edit-tex.txt` at `86ba0afa6`, "in paragraph at lines 137--155"); reordered, the build has the base's 422 overfull boxes. The words and the example are unchanged. Rejected: leaving either, a sentence of the entry broader than the chapter it describes, and a line printed into the margin.
103:17. **The interpreter's callout names the expected type among what walk does not yet do (the repair round).** Its first sentence says walk "applies the same rule at dispatch, from the run-time types of the arguments", and the rule includes the expected type (`inference.tex:80-82`, `:108-134`), which walk never uses (M2, section 4). The callout's last sentence already lists what walk does not yet do; it now begins "It does not yet fix a type parameter by the expected type" (`inference.tex:158-160`). Rung K's section adds nothing here, so the sentence holds whether K lands or not, and the replacement the gather uses if K does not land keeps it (section 6). Rejected: leaving the callout to read as if walk applied the whole rule, which the measurement contradicts; a separate callout for one clause.

Carried out on `main` after `e3a1e87ef` (the ruling, `JUDGE-review.md`), 2026-09-29, 07:38 to about 08:05 UTC, in `/home/user/fortress`, after the gate beside it had finished: every stage log under `tmp/gate-batch-N/` ends in `EXIT=0` (`compileAll.txt`, `library.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt`, `distance.txt`, `ladder-run.txt`, `microgpt-run.txt`), and no `ant` or `java` process of it was alive. `tmp/gate-batch-N/out/` was not read. Nothing was built: no file under `ProjectFortress/`, `Library/` or `Specification/` changed between rung M's commit `2770550c3`, which the gate built, and `e3a1e87ef` (`git diff --name-only 2770550c3 e3a1e87ef -- ProjectFortress Library Specification` prints nothing), and the gate's library cache served.

Corrected in the messages of `XXXInferLoneBoundUnion`, `XXXInferLoneUnionWalk` and `XXXNumeralBeyondZZ32Range`, in row 516's note and in the new `PLAN.md` line. `JUDGE-review.md` is left as the judge wrote it. The ruling's other citations were opened and hold: `inference.tex:83-98`, `:89-98`, `:95-98`, `:149-160`; `literals.tex:83-86`, `:146-148`; `conversions-coercions.tex:494-501`, `:533-553`; `conversion-overloading-judgement.md:113`; `Functionals.scala:336-343`; `EvaluatorBase.java:259-261`; `FType.java:350-380`; `TypeLatticeOps.java:30-35`.
4. **The ruling's premise for `XXXInferLoneBoundUnion` holds only in part, and the repair opens row 518 with a seventh test.** The ruling says the program "is accepted once the checker gives the union" (`JUDGE-review.md` section 1.4, "The tests"). The stand-in, `same(pick0(w, r), pick0(w, r))`, is the program as it would be after that repair, and the checker refuses it too, "(BoxT[\OR(ZZ64,RR64)\], BoxT[\OR(ZZ64,RR64)\])" (`repair-junit-standin.txt`). The stand-in is red, "Saw wrong failure", as the ruling expects, but because the compile fails with another message, not because it succeeds. Measured further (`merged-tests/RepairUnionArg.fss`, `repair-both-518.txt`): the checker refuses any call whose argument, an instance at a union, fixes a type parameter inside it: `one[\T\](a: BoxT[\T\])` called `one(pick0(w, r))` and `one(pick0(Apple, Berry))` for two plain objects; `one(pick0(w, w))` and the lone `idt(pick0(w, r))` are accepted, and walk runs all four. The specification settles it: the argument fixes the parameter by subtyping (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:75-79`), and a union is a type used for inference (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:575-581`), the type `pick0(w, r)` takes by `:95-98`. By the shared prefix's three homes and the ruling of batches 6b, 7R and 7C (`explorations/reviews/batch-7C-review.md:159`, `:179`), a defect a batch measures and the specification settles gets its expected failure in that batch. So: ledger row 518, and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXInferUnionInstanceArg.fss` with its `.test` (`compile`, pinned by `compile_err_contains`; "Saw expected failure" placed, red on the stand-in `one(pick0(w, w))`). The ruling says "It opens no row" and counts six tests; with this one the compiler tests are 883, not 882. The alternative was to record the premise's failure in row 516's note only, which leaves a defect the specification settles with no gated home, the slip the batch-7C review ruled against. `XXXInferLoneBoundUnion` is unchanged: its key names `BoxT[\Number\]`, so it goes red on a repair of row 516 whether or not row 518 is repaired, and it prints `PASS` once both are.
5. **The gate line in `RECORD.md` sits at the end of "For the gate: the run's totals".** The ruling says "at the end of its record corrections"; `RECORD.md` has no section of that name, and the line is a gate total. It names row 518's test beside the ruling's and counts six `.test` files, 877 to 883.
6. **Files beyond the ruling's list are committed:** this file; `XXXInferUnionInstanceArg.fss` and `.test` with ledger row 518 (deviation 4); `merged-tests/RepairUnionArg.fss`, the probe row 518 cites, and `merged-tests/standin-repair/forms/`, the two programs of `repair-both-forms.txt`. The new row moves every ledger line below it by one, so `FACTS.md`'s entry on the ledger's derived views is re-anchored, `fortress-gap-ledger.md:845` to `:846` (Counts by kind) and `:705` to `:706` (the revival worklist). The other files the tree holds outside the list, `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md` and `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-n/manifest/__pycache__/`, are left unstaged.

## 3. The homes of what the repair measured

- **Row 516**, the lone parameter taking a written bound (checker) or a named supertype (walk) where the chapter gives the union: home 2, `XXXInferLoneBoundUnion` and `XXXInferLoneUnionWalk`, each shown red on its stand-in.
- **Row 325**, the `MAX` face and a numeral beyond ℤ32 as a range component: home 2, the two link and `XXX` run pairs, each shown red on its stand-in. The `nat` size face stays home 3, as ruled (`JUDGE-review.md` section 2.3).
- **Row 518**, new: a union instance as the argument that fixes a type parameter, refused by the checker: home 2, `XXXInferUnionInstanceArg`, shown red on its stand-in. Its mechanism is read, not built: in the checker's subtype constraints the union cases (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:149-159`) come before the inference-variable cases (`:163-167`), so the invariant argument's `$T <: OR(ZZ64,RR64)` becomes a choice between `ZZ64` and `RR64` that the lower bounds refuse.
- **Row 76**, met again in deviation 1: already home 2 (`XXXJuxtConcatRungS`); nothing new.

## 4. For the gate

The six `.test` files and the walk file are outside the gate that ran. The push waits for a gate that includes them: `ant testFast` with 883 compiler tests (877 and one command line in each new `.test` file), and `ant testSystem` with one more interpreter file, `XXXInferLoneUnionWalk.fss`. The checker count and the distance are unaffected, since neither stage reads a test (`explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh:1-9`).

## 5. Checks

- The tracked-path loop over `JUDGE-review.md`, `RECORD.md` and this file, with `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/` in place of the rung's directory: every `compile-ladder/…` path they cite exists and is tracked once this commit lands.
- Each new test has one comment line and carries its citation in its message only; each component name appears only in its own `.fss` and `.test` files and in its stand-in.
- Items for Pavol: judge-review.1 and judge-review.3 are the rewritten row 516 line of `PLAN.md`'s "Off the path, parked"; judge-review.2 is the new line after it.

#!/bin/bash
# Every 4 minutes, if main is ahead of origin: push it to main when every unpushed commit
# touches only explorations/ (records, notes, probes); otherwise (a batch's gather has
# committed source that its gate has not yet passed) push it only to the backup branch
# wip/main-backup, so that a container reset loses nothing and main stays gated.
cd /home/user/fortress || exit 1
LOG=/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/autopush.log
while true; do
  sleep 240
  [ "$(git symbolic-ref --short HEAD 2>/dev/null)" = main ] || continue
  [ -e .git/index.lock ] && continue
  n=$(git rev-list --count origin/main..main 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
  [ "$n" -gt 0 ] || continue
  if git diff --name-only origin/main main | grep -qv '^explorations/'; then
    git push -q origin main:refs/heads/wip/main-backup 2>>/tmp/autopush.err && echo "$(date -u +%H:%M:%S) backup only, $n ahead, source touched" >> $LOG
  else
    git push -q origin main 2>>/tmp/autopush.err && git push -q origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 2>>/tmp/autopush.err && echo "$(date -u +%H:%M:%S) pushed $n" >> $LOG
  fi
done
